questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: A child who does not smile socially by 3 months and does not sit without support by 9 months has:
questions.concept: Failure to attain milestones in two or more domains defines global developmental delay. Red flags include no social smile by 3 months, no head control by 5 months, not sitting by 9 months and not walking by 18 months.

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: The core features of autism spectrum disorder are:
options: Persistent deficits in social communication with restricted repetitive behaviours
questions.concept: Autism is defined by social communication deficits plus restricted, repetitive patterns of behaviour, interests or activities, with onset in early childhood. Early behavioural intervention improves outcome; there is no association with vaccination.

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder requires symptoms to be present:
options: In more than one setting for at least six months with onset before 12 years
questions.concept: Diagnosis needs inattention and/or hyperactivity-impulsivity across at least two settings for six months with onset before age 12 and functional impairment. Behavioural therapy is first line in preschoolers; methylphenidate or atomoxetine are used in older children.

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: Nocturnal enuresis is considered abnormal and warrants evaluation after the age of:
questions.concept: Involuntary night-time wetting is normal up to 5 years. Beyond that, secondary causes such as urinary infection, diabetes, constipation and spinal dysraphism are excluded; management uses alarms, motivational therapy and desmopressin.

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: Breath-holding spells in a toddler are best managed by:
options: Reassurance with avoidance of reinforcement, after excluding iron deficiency anaemia
questions.concept: Breath-holding spells are benign, provoked by frustration or pain, and resolve by 5 years. Iron deficiency should be corrected as it increases frequency; anticonvulsants have no role since these are not seizures.
questions.reference: Ghai Essential Pediatrics 9e, Breath Holding Spells

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: The commonest nutritional problem of Indian adolescents, especially girls, is:
questions.concept: Adolescent girls have high requirements from growth and menstrual loss, so anaemia prevalence exceeds 50%. The Weekly Iron and Folic Acid Supplementation programme and Anaemia Mukt Bharat target this group.

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: Adolescence as defined by WHO covers the age group:
questions.concept: WHO defines adolescence as 10 to 19 years, youth as 15 to 24 and young people as 10 to 24 years. The Rashtriya Kishor Swasthya Karyakram addresses nutrition, mental health, injuries, substance misuse and sexual health.

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: Tourette syndrome is characterised by:
options: Multiple motor tics with at least one vocal tic persisting over a year
questions.concept: Tourette syndrome requires multiple motor and at least one vocal tic for more than a year with onset before 18 years, often with obsessive-compulsive symptoms and ADHD. Behavioural therapy is first line, with risperidone or clonidine if severe.

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: Sydenham chorea following streptococcal infection is a major criterion of:
questions.concept: Sydenham chorea is a major Jones criterion, appearing months after streptococcal infection with choreiform movements, emotional lability and hypotonia, and is self-limiting but requires secondary penicillin prophylaxis.

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: Specific learning disability such as dyslexia is characterised by:
options: Difficulty in reading despite normal intelligence and adequate schooling
questions.concept: Specific learning disability is unexpected underachievement in reading, writing or arithmetic despite normal intelligence, adequate instruction and intact senses, requiring formal psychoeducational assessment and remedial education with examination accommodations.

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: In paediatric basic life support by a single rescuer, the compression to ventilation ratio is:
options: 30 to 2 for a lay rescuer and 15 to 2 for two healthcare providers
questions.concept: A lone rescuer uses 30 to 2, while two healthcare providers use 15 to 2 in infants and children, reflecting the predominantly respiratory aetiology of paediatric arrest. Newborn resuscitation uses 3 to 1.

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: The first-line drug for a child in status epilepticus with intravenous access is:
questions.concept: A benzodiazepine - lorazepam intravenously or midazolam intranasally or buccally without access - is first line, repeated once, followed by a second-line agent such as fosphenytoin, levetiracetam or valproate if seizures persist.

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: The most reliable single sign of shock in a child is:
options: Prolonged capillary refill with tachycardia, as hypotension is a late sign
questions.concept: Children maintain blood pressure by intense vasoconstriction until late, so tachycardia, prolonged capillary refill, cool peripheries and altered mentation appear first. Hypotension signals decompensation and imminent arrest.

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: The initial fluid bolus for a child in hypovolaemic shock is:
questions.concept: Rapid boluses of 20 mL/kg normal saline or Ringer lactate are given and repeated with reassessment, though smaller 10 mL/kg boluses are used in severe malnutrition and cardiogenic shock to avoid overload.

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: Under IMNCI, a child with any general danger sign must be:
options: Referred urgently after a first dose of appropriate treatment
Treated at home with oral drugs
questions.concept: General danger signs - inability to drink or breastfeed, persistent vomiting, convulsions, lethargy or unconsciousness - mandate urgent referral with pre-referral treatment such as an antibiotic, antimalarial, or glucose and warmth.

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: Kerosene ingestion in a child is managed by:
options: Supportive care without gastric lavage or induced emesis
questions.concept: Hydrocarbons cause chemical pneumonitis if aspirated, so lavage and emesis are contraindicated. Care is supportive with oxygen and observation for respiratory distress; charcoal does not bind hydrocarbons and increases aspiration risk.

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: The commonest cause of accidental death in Indian children aged 1 to 4 years is:
questions.concept: Unintentional injury - drowning, road traffic injury, burns, falls and poisoning - is a leading cause of childhood death beyond infancy, and is addressed by supervision, home safety, helmets and child restraints.

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: Severe acute malnutrition in a child 6 to 59 months is defined by any of:
options: Weight-for-height below minus 3 SD, MUAC below 11.5 cm, or bilateral pedal oedema
questions.concept: Any one of these criteria defines severe acute malnutrition. Management follows the WHO ten steps, treating hypoglycaemia, hypothermia, dehydration, electrolytes and infection before cautious feeding to avoid refeeding syndrome.

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: In severe acute malnutrition, the rehydration fluid of choice for a dehydrated child is:
options: ReSoMal, which has lower sodium and higher potassium than standard ORS
questions.concept: Malnourished children have excess total body sodium and depleted potassium, so ReSoMal with reduced sodium, added potassium and magnesium is used orally, given slowly because of the risk of fluid overload and heart failure.

questions.subject: Pediatrics
questions.stem: The antidote for a child who has ingested an overdose of iron tablets is:
questions.concept: Iron tablets are a common and lethal accidental paediatric poisoning, causing haemorrhagic gastroenteritis, shock, hepatic necrosis and late gastric scarring. Desferrioxamine chelates free iron; charcoal is ineffective.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.topic: External & middle ear disease: otitis externa, otosclerosis
questions.stem: Malignant otitis externa most commonly occurs in and is caused by:
questions.concept: Malignant (necrotising) otitis externa is an osteomyelitis of the temporal bone in elderly diabetics or immunocompromised patients, caused by Pseudomonas aeruginosa, with granulation at the bony-cartilaginous junction and risk of facial palsy. Prolonged antipseudomonal therapy is required.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.topic: External & middle ear disease: otitis externa, otosclerosis
questions.stem: Otosclerosis characteristically causes:
options: Progressive bilateral conductive deafness with a normal tympanic membrane and paracusis willisii
questions.concept: Fixation of the stapes footplate by otosclerotic bone gives painless progressive conductive loss, often worsening in pregnancy, with a normal drum, absent stapedial reflex, Carhart's notch and paradoxically better hearing in noise (paracusis willisii).

questions.subject: ENT
questions.topic: External & middle ear disease: otitis externa, otosclerosis
questions.stem: Schwartze sign in otosclerosis refers to:
options: A reddish hue over the promontory seen through the tympanic membrane in active otospongiosis
A white patch on the drum
questions.concept: The flamingo-pink Schwartze sign reflects increased vascularity of active otospongiotic bone over the promontory, indicating an active phase where fluoride therapy may be considered.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.topic: External & middle ear disease: otitis externa, otosclerosis
questions.stem: The definitive treatment of otosclerosis with significant conductive loss is:
questions.concept: Stapedotomy with a piston prosthesis restores ossicular continuity with excellent results; a hearing aid is an alternative for those unfit or unwilling. Surgery is avoided in an only-hearing ear.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.topic: External & middle ear disease: otitis externa, otosclerosis
questions.stem: A retracted tympanic membrane with conductive deafness and a type C tympanogram in a child suggests:
options: Otitis media with effusion from eustachian tube dysfunction
questions.concept: Eustachian dysfunction, commonly from adenoid hypertrophy or allergy, causes negative middle ear pressure, retraction and serous effusion with painless hearing loss. Persistent cases need grommet insertion with adenoidectomy.
questions.reference: Dhingra ENT 7e, Otitis Media with Effusion

questions.subject: ENT
questions.topic: External & middle ear disease: otitis externa, otosclerosis
questions.stem: The commonest organism in acute suppurative otitis media is:
questions.concept: Pneumococcus, followed by Haemophilus influenzae and Moraxella catarrhalis, causes acute suppurative otitis media, usually spreading via the eustachian tube after an upper respiratory infection. Amoxicillin is first line.
questions.reference: Dhingra ENT 7e, Acute Suppurative Otitis Media

questions.subject: ENT
questions.topic: External & middle ear disease: otitis externa, otosclerosis
questions.stem: An attic (atticoantral) type of chronic suppurative otitis media is considered unsafe because it is associated with:
options: Cholesteatoma with bone erosion and intracranial complications
questions.concept: Atticoantral disease with a posterosuperior marginal perforation and cholesteatoma erodes bone by pressure and enzymatic action, causing facial palsy, labyrinthine fistula and intracranial sepsis. It requires mastoid surgery, not just medical treatment.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.topic: External & middle ear disease: otitis externa, otosclerosis
questions.stem: The tubotympanic (safe) type of chronic suppurative otitis media is characterised by:
options: A central perforation with mucoid non-offensive discharge
A marginal perforation with foul discharge
questions.concept: Safe disease shows a central perforation of the pars tensa with intermittent mucoid non-foul discharge and no bone erosion, managed by aural toilet, topical antibiotics and later tympanoplasty.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.topic: External & middle ear disease: otitis externa, otosclerosis
questions.stem: Cholesteatoma is best described as:
options: Keratinising stratified squamous epithelium in the middle ear that erodes bone
questions.concept: Despite its name, cholesteatoma contains no cholesterol and is not a tumour: it is trapped keratinising squamous epithelium producing progressive bone destruction, so the only definitive treatment is surgical removal.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.topic: External & middle ear disease: otitis externa, otosclerosis
questions.stem: Traumatic perforation of the tympanic membrane is usually managed by:
options: Keeping the ear dry and observing, as most heal spontaneously
questions.concept: Most traumatic perforations heal within weeks with dry ear precautions and avoidance of syringing and ototoxic drops. Surgery is considered only if the perforation persists beyond three months or hearing loss suggests ossicular injury.
questions.reference: Dhingra ENT 7e, Trauma to the Ear
